blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how mathematicians precisely express statements like "All humans are mortal" or "There exists a solution to this equation"? Welcome to the world of predicates and quantifiers!

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore the concepts of predicates and quantifiers, which are fundamental tools in logic and proof. Predicates allow us to express properties of objects, while quantifiers help us make statements about all or some objects in a domain.

blocks.title: Predicate
blocks.text: A predicate is a statement that contains variables and becomes a proposition when specific values are substituted for these variables. For example, $P(x)$ could represent "$x$ is a prime number."

blocks.title: Quantifiers
blocks.text: Quantifiers specify the extent to which a predicate is true over a range of elements. The two most common quantifiers are the universal quantifier ($\forall$) and the existential quantifier ($\exists$).

blocks.markdown: Let's start with the universal quantifier. The statement $\forall x, P(x)$ means "for all $x$, $P(x)$ is true." For example, "All humans are mortal" can be expressed as $\forall x, \text{Human}(x) \rightarrow \text{Mortal}(x)$.

The existential quantifier, on the other hand, is used to express that there is at least one element for which the predicate is true. The statement $\exists x, P(x)$ means "there exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$ is true." For example, "There exists a prime number greater than 10" can be expressed as $\exists x, (\text{Prime}(x) \land x > 10)$.

blocks.title: Translating English to Predicate Logic
blocks.prompt: Translate the statement "Every student in the class passed the exam" into predicate logic.

steps.text: Identify the predicate and the domain. Let $P(x)$ be the predicate "$x$ passed the exam," where $x$ is a student in the class.
Use the universal quantifier to express the statement. Since the statement is about every student, we use $\forall$.

blocks.answer: The statement is translated to $\forall x, P(x)$, where $P(x)$ is "$x$ passed the exam."

blocks.markdown: Negating quantified statements is a crucial skill. The negation of a universally quantified statement $\forall x, P(x)$ is $\exists x, \neg P(x)$, meaning "there exists an $x$ such that $P(x)$ is not true." Similarly, the negation of an existentially quantified statement $\exists x, P(x)$ is $\forall x, \neg P(x)$.

steps.text: Apply the negation rule for universally quantified statements: $\neg (\forall x, P(x)) = \exists x, \neg P(x)$.

blocks.markdown: The order of quantifiers matters significantly. For example, $\forall x \exists y, P(x, y)$ is not the same as $\exists y \forall x, P(x, y)$. The first statement means "for every $x$, there exists a $y$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true," while the second means "there exists a $y$ such that for every $x$, $P(x, y)$ is true."

blocks.title: Order of Quantifiers
blocks.text: Changing the order of quantifiers can change the meaning of a statement. Always pay attention to the sequence in which quantifiers appear.

points: Predicates and quantifiers are essential for expressing mathematical statements rigorously.
Universal quantifiers ($\forall$) and existential quantifiers ($\exists$) have distinct roles and negation rules.
The order of nested quantifiers affects the meaning of a statement.
